title: Godly Reason on Trial
sum: The speaker states his thesis: "godly reason is master in its own right over the passions" (1:1). He will prove it two ways: by argument, and from "the noble courage" of the old man Eleazar and the seven brothers and their mother, who died under the tyrant Antiochus (1:7-12). Their endurance, he says, broke the tyranny and cleansed the homeland (1:11).

Then he defines his terms like a teacher of philosophy. Reason is the mind choosing wisdom with a right way of life; wisdom is the knowledge of things divine and human, and of their causes, and it is "the training the law gives" (1:15-17). Its four kinds are good sense, justice, courage and self-restraint (1:18). The passions spring from pleasure and pain, and reason tends them like a gardener (1:20-29). The first proof is the food laws: Jews who crave forbidden foods keep away from them because reason rules (1:31-35).
readings: Read as philosophy

The chapter is a Greek lecture: thesis, definitions, divisions, proofs. Its terms (reason, passions, the four virtues, pleasure and pain) are the common stock of the schools, and its definition of wisdom is one Cicero calls the old philosophers'. Read this way, it is a Jewish thinker joining the debate about how to live.
Read as a sermon for a feast

"At this season" (1:10) suggests a speech given on a day that remembered the martyrs, perhaps at their tomb. Read this way, the philosophy is the frame and the heart is praise: the speaker wants his hearers to honor the martyrs and to live by the law as they did.

views.O: The Orthodox churches honor Eleazar, the seven brothers and their mother as the Holy Maccabees on 1 August, and the Orthodox Church in America's lives of the saints call Eleazar their teacher. A reader in that tradition hears the chapter as the opening of a feast-day oration on saints, the same kind of speech the Fathers later gave for them.
views.H: The speech is generally dated between about AD 20 and 130, most often to the first century and place it among Greek-speaking Jews outside Judea; Antioch and Alexandria have both been proposed. Eusebius and Jerome thought Josephus wrote it, but later scholars rejected that because of its language and style, its errors of history, and its outlook: Josephus favored getting along with Gentile ways, while this speech refuses any compromise. The Encyclopaedia Judaica calls it a philosophical sermon, plainly meant for delivery.
views.J: The book was not translated into Hebrew in its own era and is not in the Jewish Bible. It shows a Jewish teacher of the Greek period presenting the Torah as the true wisdom (1:17), a claim the rabbis made in their own way. The martyrs it praises entered later Jewish memory through other channels.
views.N: The speech's key words are Paul's too: the passions and cravings (Galatians 5:24; Romans 7:7), self-control (Galatians 5:23), endurance (Romans 5:3-4). Its thesis is close to the New Testament's call to rule the body, and far from it on where the power comes from (Romans 8:13).
views.G: The thesis is a theme of Greek moral philosophy: whether reason can rule the passions. The definition of wisdom (1:16) matches Cicero's report of the old philosophers; the four virtues (1:18) are Plato's; the sorting of the passions by pleasure and pain (1:20-23) follows the Stoics. The speaker departs from the Stoics in letting reason rule rather than uproot (1:6), and he makes the law of Moses the school of wisdom (1:17).
views.W: Catholic and Protestant churches do not count 4 Maccabees as Scripture; Jerome did not include it in the Vulgate. They can read the chapter as a witness to how Jews in the Greek world explained their faith, and to the language of virtue that later Christian teaching took up (the Catholic Catechism's four cardinal virtues, Catechism 1805).

deep.b: The speaker tells his hearers where he is going. First he will show from the nature of reason and the passions, and from examples in the law, that godly reason rules (1:13-3:18). Then he will turn "to my account of them" (1:12), the martyrs, whose deaths are the stronger proof (1:7-9). The plan holds: the history begins at 3:19, Eleazar's death ends with a first conclusion (6:31-35), and the same formula of the thesis returns at the end of the brothers' story (13:1) and in the last appeal (18:2).

deep.h: Reason, the passions and the four virtues
deep.b: Each term comes from Greek philosophy, but the speaker fills it with the law. Reason (logismos) is the mind at work, joined to a right life (1:15); Codex Sinaiticus and Venetus say "right reason", the Stoic phrase. Wisdom is "the knowledge of things divine and human, and of their causes", the definition Cicero says the old philosophers gave (On Duties 2.5), and it is "the training the law gives" (1:17). The four virtues, good sense, justice, courage and self-restraint, are those of Plato's good city (Republic 4.427e). The passions come from pleasure and pain (1:20), as the Stoics taught; but where the Stoics wanted the wise man free of passions, the speaker says reason rules them "not so as to destroy them" (1:6).

echoes: Galatians 5:22-24; Romans 7:7-8; Wisdom of Solomon 8:7; Proverbs 1:7; Deuteronomy 4:6; Leviticus 11; Deuteronomy 14:3-20; 2 Maccabees 6:18-7:42

settings.what: The opening of the speech: thesis and plan
settings.by: The speaker, an unnamed Jewish teacher (Eusebius and Jerome named Josephus)
settings.to: His hearers, addressed as "you", gathered "at this season" (1:10)
settings.when: Perhaps at a commemoration of the martyrs
settings.why: To win their full attention for a philosophical proof, and to announce the praise of Eleazar, the seven brothers and their mother. Knowing that the hearers honored these martyrs explains why the philosophy is always pointed toward them.

views: Moses Hadas argued for Antioch in Syria: a Greek city with a large Jewish minority, where Christians later honored churches of the Maccabean martyrs, and the book's words are rare in Alexandrian writings such as 3 Maccabees. The Encyclopaedia Judaica suggests an assembly at the martyrs' supposed tomb, perhaps at Antioch, on a day of remembrance.

Alexandria was the largest center of Jewish writing in Greek, but Hans Freudenthal and Eduard Norden judged the book's outlook hard to fit there. Judea is unlikely, because of the Greek and the audience it assumes.

Elias Bickerman about AD 20-54; Moses Hadas about AD 40; David deSilva (in James Rochford's summary of his argument) the first half of the first century, since Syria, Phoenicia and Cilicia were joined into one unit at some point between AD 19 and 72 (4:2); André Dupont-Sommer under Hadrian (AD 118-135); Jan Willem van Henten a wider range, with the last decades of the first century as plausible.

settings.what: The argument from reason and the law
settings.when: The first, philosophical half of the speech
settings.why: To prove the thesis from definitions and from examples in the law of Moses before turning to the martyrs, so that hearers schooled in Greek ideas see that the law is the true philosophy.

title: The Law That Trains the Mind
sum: The speaker gathers proofs from the law. Joseph, young and in his prime, mastered desire (2:1-4). The tenth commandment forbids craving, so reason must be able to rule it (2:5-6). The laws on loans without interest, the release of debts, gleaning, family loyalty and even kindness to enemies all train reason against greed, stinginess, family love and hatred (2:7-14). Moses settled his anger by reason, and Jacob cursed the anger of Simeon and Levi, which he would not have done if anger could not be ruled (2:15-20).

The chapter's center is a short account of creation: God planted the passions in the human being, set the mind on its throne as "the holy leader", and gave it the law; the mind that lives by it reigns over a kingdom of the four virtues (2:21-23). Then the old objection returns: why does reason not rule forgetting? (2:24).
readings: Read as a lesson in the law
Each law is chosen to show a passion being trained: lending trains generosity, gleaning trains a stingy man, the war laws train a hater. The law of Moses is a curriculum for the soul.
Read beside Romans 7

Paul quotes the same commandment and says it awakened every kind of craving in him (Romans 7:7-8). Set side by side, the two passages are two Jewish readings of one law: one confident that the law strengthens reason, the other that the law shows sin and cannot overcome it.

views.H: The examples come from the Greek Bible: the quotation of the tenth commandment follows its Greek word for word in its first and last clauses. The speaker does not argue from the text of each law but uses them as moral training, the way Greek-speaking Jewish writers presented the law to outsiders.
views.J: The use of the law as moral training fits a long Jewish tradition, and the speaker's Moses and Jacob are figures of restraint. The Torah's own reasons for these laws (the poor, the foreigner, the LORD's ownership of the land) are left aside in favor of the training of reason.
views.N: The comparison with Romans 7-8 is the main one: "The law, then, is holy" (Romans 7:12), Paul agrees, but "The law was powerless, because the flesh made it weak" (Romans 8:3). Where 4 Maccabees says reason rules the passions through the law, Paul says believers "put to death the deeds of the body by the Spirit" (Romans 8:13).
views.G: The picture of the mind enthroned as "the holy leader" (2:22) uses the philosophers' word hēgemōn, "leader", for the ruling part of the soul. The idea that reason should rule the lower parts of the soul like a king is old in Greek thought; the speaker makes the law the king's charter.
views.W: Catholic and Protestant readers have debated the very question the chapter raises: what the law can do, and what needs grace. The card below sets out their answers.

deep.b: 2:21-23 is the place where 4 Maccabees is furthest from Paul. For the speaker, God gave the mind the law at creation, and "If the mind lives by that law, it will be king" (2:23). Nothing in the chapter speaks of a fall or of sin's power over the will. For Paul, the same commandment "You must not crave" showed him what craving was (Romans 7:7), and "in the parts of my body I see another law" that takes him prisoner (Romans 7:23); the answer is not reason but "God did what it could not" (Romans 8:3). Fairly put, the two do not disagree that the law is good, nor that the passions must be ruled. They disagree on whether the human mind, taught by the law, has the strength to rule them. Both readings honor the law, and both have Jewish roots: Sirach too says, "If you are willing, you will keep the commandments" (Sirach 15:15).

echoes: Genesis 39:7-12; Exodus 20:17; Deuteronomy 5:21; Romans 7:7-8; Deuteronomy 15:1-2; Leviticus 19:9-10; Deuteronomy 13:6-10; Deuteronomy 20:19; Exodus 23:4-5; Numbers 16:12-15; Genesis 34:25-31; Genesis 49:5-7; Romans 8:3; Sirach 15:14-15

settings.what: Laws cited as training for reason (the tenth commandment; loans, gleaning, family, enemies)
settings.by: The speaker, citing the law of Moses
settings.to: His hearers; the laws themselves bound every Israelite: households, lenders, landowners, soldiers in war
settings.when: In the philosophical half of the speech
settings.why: The laws were given to Israel in the land: release of debts every seventh year, gleanings for the poor and foreigner, care for an enemy's animals and trees. The speaker uses them to show that a person who keeps them must rule greed, stinginess, love and hatred. Knowing whom the laws bound shows how ordinary the training is: it happens in fields and loans, not in a school.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews of the Diaspora, in the first century AD or a little later. The speech's Greek, its philosophy and its retelling of 2 Maccabees point to a Jewish community at home in Greek culture. The date and place are debated (see the views).

traditions.q: 4 Maccabees says the mind that lives by God's law can rule every passion (2:21-23; 3:2-5). Can reason trained by the law master sin's desires, or does it take grace? (Whether the human will is free is asked at Romans 9; whether a Christian can reach perfection, at Matthew 5; who the "I" of Romans 7 is, at Romans 7.)
views: Not without grace, though human effort is real. No one is justified "by his own works, whether done through the teaching of human nature, or that of the law, without the grace of God through Jesus Christ" (Trent, session 6, canon 1); yet the commandments are not "impossible to keep" for one who is justified and in grace (canon 18). The moral virtues "are acquired by human effort" and "order our passions", but they "are purified and elevated by divine grace", and since it is not easy for one "wounded by sin" to keep moral balance, Christ's gift offers "the grace necessary to persevere" (Catechism 1804, 1810-1811).

Reason keeps real power, but spiritual good needs grace. The Synod of Jerusalem (1672) teaches that fallen man kept "free-will, living and operating, so that he is by nature able to choose and do what is good"; yet good done "by nature only" "does not itself contribute to salvation without faith", and "for the regenerated to do spiritual good ... it is necessary that he be guided and prevented [preceded] by grace" (Confession of Dositheus, decree 14).

Reason can rule outward conduct, not the heart before God. The will "has some liberty to choose civil righteousness" and to work "things subject to reason", but "it has no power, without the Holy Ghost, to work the righteousness of God, that is, spiritual righteousness"; the Pelagians are condemned for teaching that "without the Holy Ghost, by the power of nature alone" one can love God above all (Augsburg Confession 18).

No. Fallen man "hath wholly lost all ability of will to any spiritual good accompanying salvation" (Westminster Confession 9.3); God's grace alone enables the converted to will what is good, yet "by reason of his remaining corruption" he still wills evil too (9.4). Believers' "ability to do good works is not at all of themselves, but wholly from the Spirit of Christ" (16.3).

By grace, not by reason, and not without limits. John Wesley taught that Christians are "so far perfect, as not to commit sin" (Sermon 40, "Christian Perfection", 2.20) and that those grown strong in faith are "freed from evil thoughts and evil tempers" (2.21), because Christ has "purified their hearts by faith" (2.26). The same sermon says this perfection does not mean freedom "either from ignorance or mistake, or infirmities or temptations" (1.9): a cleansing of the heart by grace, not mastery by reason.

title: David Pours Out the Water
sum: After answering the objection, the speaker states his principle: no one can cut out craving, anger or malice, but reason can keep a person from being their slave; reason is not the one who uproots the passions but the one who wrestles them (3:1-5).

The proof is King David. After a day of battle he craves water from the enemy's camp; two young soldiers slip through the lines and bring it from the spring; and David, judging that it was bought with blood, sets reason against his craving and pours it out to God (3:6-18). Then the speaker turns to history: in a time of deep peace, when even King Seleucus paid for the temple service, some men started a revolt against the people's harmony (3:19-21).
readings: Read as a moral example
David is the strongest case: a king, exhausted and burning with thirst, with the water already in his hands. If reason can rule there, it can rule anywhere.
Read beside Samuel

In 2 Samuel 23:13-17 David honors the courage of three warriors who risked their lives; the point is loyalty and the sacredness of life. 4 Maccabees moves the point inward: the victory is over David's own craving.

views.H: The retelling changes the details of 2 Samuel 23:13-17 (two young soldiers instead of three warriors; a spring in the camp instead of the well at Bethlehem's gate; the scene after a battle) and adds psychology. The history that begins at 3:19 follows 2 Maccabees 3, but the king's name, "Seleucus Nicanor", is a slip for Seleucus IV.
views.J: David's refusal to drink is remembered in the Bible as an act of reverence: the water was like the blood of the men, and blood belongs to God (Leviticus 17:11). The speaker keeps that reasoning (3:15) and adds his own.
views.N: The wrestling language of 3:5 and 3:18 begins the book's picture of the moral life as a contest, which Hebrews also uses: "Not yet have you held out to the point of blood in your fight against sin" (Hebrews 12:4). Paul calls his own coming death a drink offering (Philippians 2:17).
views.G: "Reason is not the one who pulls up the passions by the roots" (3:5) is the book's sharpest word against the Stoic ideal of a wise man free of passions. Reason here is a wrestler and a ruler that keeps the passions in check, not a surgeon that removes them.

echoes: 2 Samuel 23:13-17; 1 Chronicles 11:15-19; Leviticus 17:10-14; Philippians 2:17; Hebrews 12:4; 2 Maccabees 3:1-3

settings.what: The history: from peace to persecution
settings.when: The turn from argument to the martyrs ("Now the time calls us", 3:19)
settings.why: To set the stage for the martyrs: a law-keeping people at peace, betrayed from within, then forced by a tyrant to eat defiling food. The short history shows that the martyrs died for the very law the first half praised.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews of the Diaspora, in the first century AD or a little later. The speech's Greek, its philosophy and its retelling of 2 Maccabees point to a Jewish community at home in Greek culture. The date and place are debated (see the views).

title: From Betrayal to Persecution
sum: Simon, a rival of the high priest Onias, betrays his homeland to Apollonius, governor of Syria, Phoenicia and Cilicia, with a tale of private money in the temple treasuries (4:1-6). Apollonius comes with an army, the people pray, and angels on horseback appear from heaven; Apollonius falls half dead, begs for prayer, and Onias prays for him (4:7-14).

When Seleucus dies, Antiochus Epiphanes takes the throne and sells the high priesthood to Onias's brother Jason, who builds a gymnasium and ends the care of the temple (4:15-20). Divine Justice makes war on Antiochus. When the people of Jerusalem rejoice at a false report of his death, he plunders them and decrees death for anyone who keeps the law. When even mothers die for circumcising their babies, he sets out to force each Jew by torture to taste defiling food (4:21-26).
readings: Read as history

The chapter is a short version of 2 Maccabees 3-6, with real people (Onias III, Jason, Antiochus IV) and real events (the sale of the high priesthood, the gymnasium, the decrees of 167 BC). It also has errors: Antiochus was Seleucus's brother, not his son, and Apollonius takes Heliodorus's part.
Read as the setting of a contest
For the speech, the history is only the stage. Its point is that the law itself was outlawed, so that every Jew had to choose between the law and life. That is the test the martyrs will pass.

views.O: The Orthodox calendar remembers the Holy Maccabees on 1 August; this chapter's history explains why they died. The story of heaven defending the temple (4:10) stands beside other accounts of angels guarding God's house.
views.H: Compared point by point with 2 Maccabees: Simon goes to Apollonius as in 2 Maccabees 3:5, but here Apollonius, not Heliodorus, goes to Jerusalem; the riders become angels; Onias prays rather than sacrifices; Antiochus is called Seleucus's son; the price of the high priesthood is 3,660 talents instead of 360 plus 80; the gymnasium is "on top of" the citadel, not at its foot. The title of Apollonius (4:2) may reflect the Roman provinces of the writer's day, which some use to date the book.
views.J: The persecution of 167 BC is the background of Hanukkah, and Ewald and Freudenthal thought the speech a Hanukkah homily. The rededication of the temple, the center of 1 and 2 Maccabees, is not told here at all: the speech is about the martyrs, not the victory.
views.N: The temple court "open to all peoples" (4:11) is the court where Gentiles might stand; Paul was mobbed when people thought he had "brought Greeks into the temple" (Acts 21:28). Many readers take Daniel 11:28-31 as a prophecy of these events and connect it with Jesus' warning in Mark 13:14.
views.W: Catholic and Protestant readers who do not count 4 Maccabees as Scripture can still read the chapter as a witness to how the persecution was remembered two centuries later.

deep.b: 4:1-26 compresses 2 Maccabees 3:1-6:11. Kept: a time of peace when the king paid for the sacrifices (2 Maccabees 3:1-3); Simon's quarrel with Onias and his report of private money (2 Maccabees 3:4-6); prayers in the temple; a heavenly attack; the high priest's fear that the king might suspect a plot, and his intercession (2 Maccabees 3:31-33); Jason's purchase of the office and his gymnasium (2 Maccabees 4:7-15); the false rumor of the king's death and the sack of Jerusalem (2 Maccabees 5:5-11); the mothers killed with their circumcised babies (2 Maccabees 6:10). Changed: Apollonius replaces Heliodorus; the rider and two young men become angels on horseback; Onias prays but offers no sacrifice; Antiochus becomes Seleucus's son; the price becomes 3,660 talents; the king himself tortures each Jew (4:26). Left out: Menelaus, Jason's attack on the city, the temple given to Zeus. The Encyclopaedia Judaica judges that what is not from 2 Maccabees came from the author's imagination.

echoes: 2 Maccabees 3:1-40; 2 Maccabees 4:7-17; 2 Maccabees 5:5-14; 2 Maccabees 6:1-11; 1 Maccabees 1:10-64; Daniel 11:21-31; Acts 21:28

settings.why: To win the king's favor by pointing him to money he could seize, presenting it as private and so not sacred. The lie is the first step toward the persecution.

settings.why: He confesses his sin and begs them to pray for him, promising to tell everyone how blessed the place is: the temple's God has defended it, and even the enemy admits it.

title: The Tyrant and the Old Priest
sum: Antiochus takes his seat with his counselors and armed troops and orders every Hebrew to be forced to taste pork and food sacrificed to idols, on pain of the wheel. The first brought before him is Eleazar, a priest, an expert in the law and an old man (5:1-4). The king speaks like a philosopher: he respects the old man's age, but no philosopher would refuse nature's gift of pork, and any god would forgive what is done under force (5:5-13).

Eleazar answers with a speech. His people live by a divine law; even if it were not divine they could not throw away their name for godliness; a small sin weighs the same as a great one (5:16-21). The law is the true philosophy, teaching self-restraint, courage, justice and godliness, and the Creator who made nature gave the law to fit it (5:22-26). Let the king prepare his wheels and fire: Eleazar will not betray the law, his self-control, his reason or his priesthood, and the fathers will welcome him pure (5:27-38).
readings: Read as a philosophical debate

Two speeches face each other: the king's argument from nature, pleasure and common sense, and Eleazar's argument from the divine law, reputation and the unity of virtue. The speaker lets the king argue well, so that the answer counts.
Read as a martyr's confession

Eleazar's speech is also a confession of faith before a ruler, like those of Daniel's friends (Daniel 3:16-18) and the apostles (Acts 5:29). Its last lines are a farewell to everything he loves: the law, self-control, reason, the priesthood.

views.O: The Orthodox Church in America's lives of the saints remember Eleazar as the teacher of the seven brothers. His defense of the law before the king is honored as the confession of a righteous one of the Old Testament.
views.H: 2 Maccabees 6:18-31 gives Eleazar a short speech about his age and example. 4 Maccabees gives the king a speech of his own and turns Eleazar's answer into a defense of the law as philosophy. The speeches are the writer's: they show how a Greek-speaking Jew of his day would answer the Greek charge that the food laws were against reason and nature.
views.J: The question whether one may break the law to save one's life was later answered by the rabbis: in general yes, but not for idolatry, forbidden sexual relations or bloodshed, and in a time of persecution not even for a minor command (Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 74a). Eleazar's stand, in public and under a decree, fits that ruling, and his words that small and great sins weigh the same match Mishnah Avot 2:1.
views.N: "Someone might keep the entire law and trip over only one command, but he has become answerable for all of it" (James 2:10) is close to 5:20. The early church faced the same choice before rulers (Acts 4:19; Acts 5:29), and many Christians read Mark 7:19 and Romans 14:14 as setting the food laws aside, though Messianic Jewish and other Torah-observant readers take those verses differently.
views.G: The king's case is popular Stoicism: live by nature, enjoy pleasures that bring no shame. Eleazar answers in kind: the law teaches the virtues (5:23-24), and its Creator made it fit nature (5:25). He calls the law "our philosophy" (5:22) and addresses "reason, lover of wisdom" (5:35).

deep.h: The law as reason's own philosophy
deep.b: Antiochus's charge is that Judaism is not philosophy: a wise man would follow nature, which made pork good to eat (5:7-11). Eleazar's answer has three steps. First, obedience: the law is divine, so no force is stronger than obedience to it (5:16-17), and even if it were not, a man's good name for godliness could not be thrown away (5:18). Second, virtue: the law trains all four virtues and godliness besides (5:23-24), so to live by it is to live by reason ("as if our life by it had no sound reason in it", 5:22). Third, nature: the Creator who made the world gave the law, so it fits our nature; he allowed what suits the soul and forbade what works against it (5:25-26). The speaker thus turns the Greek ideal of life according to nature into a defense of the Torah.

echoes: 2 Maccabees 6:18-28; Daniel 3:16-18; Acts 4:19; Acts 5:29; James 2:10; Matthew 5:19; Deuteronomy 14:8; Leviticus 11:7

settings.to: Eleazar, before the king's counselors and troops
settings.why: To win the old man by flattery and philosophy rather than force: respect for his age, the argument from nature, and the promise that any god would forgive. In the story it is a real temptation; for the hearers it states the Greek case against the food laws at its strongest.

settings.by: Eleazar, a priest and expert in the law
settings.when: Given permission to speak, facing the wheel and the fire
settings.why: To defend the law as divine, reasonable and fitting to nature, and to declare that he will not break it. For the speech's hearers it is a model answer to Greek critics and a call to the same loyalty.

title: A Life in Exchange
sum: The guards strip the old man, bind him and whip him while a herald shouts "Obey the king's commands!" He falls, but keeps his reason upright; like a noble athlete he defeats his torturers (6:1-11). Some of the king's men, out of pity and old friendship, offer him cooked meat so that he can pretend to eat pork. He refuses: an old man who pretended would teach the young ungodliness and live a little longer in shame (6:12-23).

They take him to the fire. Burned to the bone, he lifts his eyes to God: "Be merciful to your nation. Let the penalty we pay on their account be enough for you. Make my blood their cleansing, and take my soul as a life in exchange for them" (6:28-29). He dies, holding firm by reason. The speaker draws his first conclusion: godly reason is master over the passions, both pains and pleasures (6:31-35).
readings: Read as a proof
For the speech, Eleazar's death is evidence: a body broken and burned, a reason that does not bend. The conclusion follows at once (6:31).
Read as a sacrifice

An old priest dies praying that his blood will cleanse the nation and his soul be taken as a life in exchange for them. Read this way the chapter is about atonement: a martyr's death offered to God for others, which the speech returns to at 17:20-22.

views.O: The Orthodox churches honor Eleazar among the Holy Maccabees on 1 August. The question of whether their sufferings atoned for others is set out on the 2 Maccabees 7 card.
views.H: 2 Maccabees 6:18-31 tells Eleazar's death without a prayer for the nation; that prayer is 4 Maccabees' own. Its words for cleansing (katharsion) and exchange (antipsychon) belong to Greek ideas of a death that saves a city, and Jan Willem van Henten argues that the books join that Greek language to Hebrew ideas of atonement.
views.J: The prayer draws on Israel's own Scriptures: blood that makes atonement by the life in it (Leviticus 17:11), the servant who bore the sin of many (Isaiah 53:12), Moses offering himself for the people (Exodus 32:32). Van Henten calls the idea of one dying for others "marginal" in early Jewish writings after the Bible, which makes this prayer stand out.
views.N: The likeness to the New Testament is close: "a ransom in place of many" (Mark 10:45), "my blood of the covenant ... poured out for many" (Mark 14:24), "the place of atonement ... by his blood" (Romans 3:25). Whether Jesus' first followers knew this book is not shown; the shared background is the idea of a righteous death for others.
views.G: The athlete (6:10), the noble death and the contest are Greek pictures, and the endurance of pain is a test of the philosopher. The speaker's conclusion uses the language of the law court: "Beyond all doubt" (6:31).
views.W: For Catholic and Protestant churches the book is not Scripture. Both read Eleazar's prayer as a witness to Jewish hope that God would accept the faithful dead for the nation, and both hold that Christ's death alone is the atoning sacrifice; they differ on whether believers' sufferings share in it (the 2 Maccabees 7 card).

deep.b:
The words. Eleazar asks three things. "Be merciful" (hileōs genou) is the plea of Moses for the people in the Greek of Exodus 32:12. "Let the penalty we pay on their account be enough for you" asks God to count the martyrs' suffering as the punishment the nation deserved; Codex Sinaiticus has hyper, "on their behalf", for peri, "on their account" (see the variant). "Make my blood their cleansing" (katharsion, a purifying offering) and "take my soul as a life in exchange for them" (antipsychon, a life given in place of a life) are the strongest words: his death is to work like a sacrifice and a substitute.

The Jewish background. The law says, "It is the blood that makes atonement, by means of the life in it" (Leviticus 17:11). The servant of Isaiah "was pierced because of our rebellions" and "bore the sin of many" (Isaiah 53:5, 12). Moses offered himself: "But if not, wipe me out, please, from your book" (Exodus 32:32). In 2 Maccabees the youngest brother prays God "to be gracious soon to the nation" and "in me and my brothers to stop the anger of the Almighty" (2 Maccabees 7:37-38). 4 Maccabees goes further: the death itself is offered as cleansing and exchange, and the speech says at the end that through the martyrs the homeland was cleansed (1:11; 17:21-22). Jan Willem van Henten writes that in 2 Maccabees 7:37-38 Greek words about death for one's fatherland are "combined for the first time with conceptions about atonement in the Hebrew Bible", and that "In early post-biblical Jewish literature, the idea of a vicarious death remains marginal" (The Maccabean Martyrs as Saviours of the Jewish People, 157, 160, in the passages Neil Godfrey quotes).

The Christian readings. For the New Testament, the one death that cleanses and ransoms is Jesus': "the blood of Jesus his Son makes us clean from every sin" (1 John 1:7); he came "to give his life as a ransom in place of many" (Mark 10:45); he "offered himself flawless to God" (Hebrews 9:14). Whether the faithful's sufferings can share in that is asked on the 2 Maccabees 7 card, top martyrs.

Did these verses shape the New Testament? The words are close, and many readers set 6:28-29 and 17:20-22 beside Romans 3:25 and Mark 10:45. Wikipedia's article on 4 Maccabees, citing David deSilva's guide to the book (1998), describes it as proposing that the sacrifice of animals could be replaced by the "obedience unto death" of faithful people. Others are cautious: Daniel Bailey warns against "paralleling Romans and 4 Maccabees prematurely", since the key word may mean different things in each. Proposed dates for the book run from about AD 20 to the early second century (see 4:2), so it may be earlier or later than Mark and Paul, and any link may run through shared ideas rather than through the book itself.

deep.title: Why make Eleazar a priest? (Claude's theory)
deep.b: This is my own suggestion. 2 Maccabees calls Eleazar a scribe (2 Maccabees 6:18); 4 Maccabees calls him "a priest by birth" (5:4), "honored priesthood" is the last thing he refuses to betray (5:35), and the speaker calls him "the holy man" (hieros, the word of temple things) just after his prayer (6:30). Only in 4 Maccabees does he pray for his blood to cleanse the nation (6:29). I suggest the writer made him a priest so that his death could be heard as a priest's offering: the one who once offered the people's sacrifices now offers himself. None of the sources opened for this part makes this argument.

settings.what: The king's men offer a way out
settings.by: Some of the king's men who had known Eleazar
settings.to: Eleazar, beaten and on the ground
settings.why: Out of pity and old friendship they offer him the chance to pretend. The offer is kind, which makes it the harder temptation.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews of the Diaspora, in the first century AD or a little later. The speech's Greek, its philosophy and its retelling of 2 Maccabees point to a Jewish community at home in Greek culture. The date and place are debated (see the views).

settings.to: The king's men, and through them "Abraham's children" (6:17, 22) and the guards (6:23)
settings.why: To show that pretending would teach the young ungodliness and buy only a short, shameful life; and to call all Jews to die nobly for godliness. For the hearers it is an example of public faithfulness.
